_comment: Which prebuilt RTL8812EU kernel-module flavor serves which board profile.
`driver-matrix.json` says WHICH KERNELS CI builds a module for. This file
says WHICH BOARDS each of those kernels serves, and — just as important —
which boards deliberately have no prebuilt at all. `tests/test_driver_coverage.py`
keeps the two in step: every board profile under src/ados/hal/boards/ must be
classified here exactly once, every flavor named here must exist in the matrix,
and every matrix row must be named here. So adding a board, renaming a flavor
or deleting a row fails CI instead of silently costing a board its fast path.
Coverage is per KERNEL IMAGE, not per board: one row serves every board that
runs that kernel. A board whose kernel is not in the matrix still works — it
falls back to the on-device DKMS build (several minutes) instead of fetching
`builds_on_device` is a first-class answer, not a backlog. We do not publish
kernel modules for hardware we cannot test on.

cubie-a7z: Mapped to radxa-a733 because that row builds the Allwinner A733 BSP kernel
(5.15.147-21-a733) both A733 boards run on the Radxa bullseye image.
An Armbian community image for the same silicon runs a DIFFERENT kernel
(6.6.98-vendor-sun60iw2) which this row does NOT cover — a module must
vermagic-match exactly, and same-SoC is not same-kernel. That kernel is
deliberately left on the DKMS fallback: its headers are published only on
the Armbian BETA feed (linux-headers-vendor-sun60iw2; absent from the
stable feed entirely), and monitor-mode injection is broken on it anyway,
so a prebuilt module would build fast and still not carry a radio link.
Adding it later means a new matrix row pointing at the beta feed.
builds_on_device: No matrix row: either the kernel line is not one we run, or we have no
unit of that board to validate a published module against. These boards
compile the driver locally at install time and work; they are just slower
to provision. Moving one out of this list means adding a matrix row AND
confirming the built module loads on real hardware.
